c1.story:
Next time you are in a hospital, look at the back of your hand. The little plastic tube taped there, the IV cannula, has a decent chance of having been made in Faridabad. Poly Medicure, which started out making exactly such disposables, now ships them to hospitals across the world. Look around the ward and you will see everything else a doctor touches that is not a medicine: syringes, catheters, blood-collection tubes, test kits, dental fillings, BP monitors, and, in the basement, the giant MRI scanner. That is the medical devices industry.

Here is the twist that shapes everything on this page. The expensive end, the scanners, cath labs, pacemakers, orthopaedic implants, is still largely imported, made by multinationals like GE, Siemens, Philips, Medtronic and Abbott. The listed Indian companies live almost entirely at the cheap, high-volume end. So when you buy an Indian device stock, you are rarely buying a technology story. You are buying a manufacturing-cost story.

Within that, there are three doors. The first is the disposables maker: single-use items made by the million in sterile plants, sold to Indian hospitals and to distributors abroad. Poly Medicure, Prevest in dental materials, and peers behind this door win on volume, sterility and cost per unit. Think of a factory making paper cups for every tea stall in the country.

The second door sells to laboratories: plastic tips and tubes from Tarsons, glassware from Borosil Scientific, molecular test kits from the company once known as Kilitch Drugs. Their customers are research labs, pharma quality-control labs and pathology chains, and their demand has a memory of Covid that has not fully faded.

The third door is the trader or contract assembler: companies like Nureca that import or assemble home-care gadgets and sell them under a brand, or make lenses and health products for someone else's label.

In Indian medtech, the moat is not a patent. It is a sterile plant, a regulator's approval and a lower cost than China.

Each door responds differently to the same news. A US tariff on Chinese syringes is a gift to door one. A pharma lab cutting spending hurts door two. A cheaper Chinese gadget on an e-commerce site hurts door three, and only door three.
c1.read:
The three tiles above are the three doors. Read each from top to bottom.

  • The name and the line under it tell you how the product is sold: by the million to hospitals and foreign distributors; to research, pharma and pathology labs; or as imported or assembled products under a brand.
  • The tickers are listed names behind that door. Click one to open its stock page. Notice how small most of these companies are; the so-what line under the tiles says it plainly: the listed universe is almost all low-technology, small-cap.
  • The bar shows how much of the profit the company keeps. Disposables makers sit at medium: they own plants and approvals, but hospitals and tenders buy on price. Lab tools also sit at medium, with a moat in quality and qualification but exposure to lab spending swings. Traders and contract makers sit at low, because anyone can import the same box from the same Chinese factory.
  • The last line is the bet: hospital volumes and a cost edge over China for door one; pharma and research spending for door two; distribution reach and import prices for door three.

The test for any name: find its gross margin. A maker with real plants usually earns a high one; a trader, a thin one. If the margin looks like a trader's but the company calls itself a manufacturer, read the annual report's description of its plants before anything else. Card four shows why that single number sorts the doors so cleanly.

c2.story:
Follow a single IV cannula backwards from the patient's hand and you find a kitchen with five stations, most of them outside India.

Station one is the pantry: medical-grade plastics, stainless-steel needle tubing, electronic components, sensors and chips. India imports much of it, China first, then Europe and the US. Even a domestic disposables maker buys a good part of its polymer abroad, and a gadget maker buys nearly all its electronics.

Station two is moulding and sub-assembly: plastic parts shot out of moulds, needles ground to a point, circuit boards populated. China does this at a scale no one else matches, but a growing set of Indian makers is setting up here, many of them inside the new device parks.

Station three is where India's listed companies stand: final assembly, sterilisation and packing into a finished device that a regulator has approved. This is the step that turns a plastic part into a medical product, and the step that carries the licence. Multinationals also have plants here, mostly for implants and machines.

Station four is distribution and procurement, a maze of distributors, hospital purchase departments, state medical corporations, the government e-marketplace, GeM, and export agents. Public tenders usually reward the lowest bid.

Station five is the user: the hospital, the pathology lab, the dentist, and the patient at home with a glucometer, who uses the device once and throws it away.

India imports somewhere between two-thirds and three-quarters of the devices it uses, the high-value machines and implants among them. Delhi's response, through the device incentive scheme and parks in Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Himachal, is to pull more of stations one and two onshore. The Andhra Pradesh MedTech Zone in Visakhapatnam was the early flagship of that push. Progress is real at the disposables end and slow at the high-tech end.
c2.read:
Read the five boxes left to right, then the two band rows below.

The boxes are the stations, from raw materials on the left to the user on the right. Only station three is highlighted, because that is the single station where India's listed names stand: POLYMED, PREVEST, TARSONS, BOROSCI and peers, assembling and sterilising finished devices. Compare that with pharma, where Indian companies hold two stations; here they hold one.

The first band row labels who holds each station. The first two cells are coloured as rival: Imports and China at station one, China and India at station two, where Indian moulders are starting to compete. India listed sits at three. Distributors and tenders at four, hospitals and labs at five.

The second band row shows China's reach, drawn across the first four stations with the last cell marked World. China's grip is strongest on the left, in components and moulding, and its finished devices compete with India's at stations three and four, on hospital tenders and in export markets.

Now read the so-what under the diagram: station one is the cost line. Because an Indian maker buys much of its polymer and electronics abroad, a weaker rupee or a Chinese component price change hits margins within a quarter.

Use the map to place every headline. A polymer price rise lands at station one. A new device park subsidy aims at stations one and two. A price cap lands at four. A US tariff on Chinese devices reshuffles who wins at three and four.

c3.story:
A syringe has no brand loyalty and no fashion cycle. It is used once and thrown away. That makes the disposables business wonderfully predictable at its core: every occupied hospital bed consumes cannulas, catheters, syringes and tubing every single day.

The private hospital chains are the steady base. As Apollo, Max, Medanta and their peers open the largest pipeline of new beds in a decade, each new bed becomes a daily customer for disposables from the day it opens. Rising insurance penetration means more surgery, and surgery is disposable-heavy.

Government hospitals buy through tenders, mostly syringes, kits and basic disposables. Volumes are huge but margins thin, because tenders reward the lowest bid. Local-content rules give Indian makers a preference, which helps.

Export distributors in Europe, the US and emerging markets buy infusion and vascular-access products. Here the driver is China+1: hospital buyers who want a supplier outside China. In 2024 Washington sharply raised tariffs on Chinese syringes and needles, and that kind of decision redirects orders toward Indian plants over the following quarters.

Then the lab customers, and this is where the volatility lives. Pharma and biotech labs buy plasticware and glassware for research and quality control; pathology and molecular labs buy test kits and collection tubes. During Covid, both bought like there was no tomorrow, and labs and distributors over-ordered for fear of shortages. Then demand vanished and they sat on stock for nearly two years. Tarsons, which listed in 2021 near the top of that frenzy, lived through both sides.

Dentists and clinics buy filling materials and cements, a demand tied to urban incomes and cosmetic dentistry. And households buy BP monitors, glucometers, nebulisers and spectacle lenses, mostly online, where a cheaper import is always one click away.

A hospital bed is a subscription. An outbreak is a sugar rush. Never confuse the two.
c3.read:
Each tile is one customer group. Read every tile in three lines.

  • The name is who is buying.
  • The second line is what they buy: disposables and implants, tendered basics, infusion and vascular-access exports, lab plasticware, test kits, dental materials, home devices.
  • The third line is what moves that customer. This is your watchlist beyond the company.

The useful way to read this grid is to sort the tiles into steady and swinging. Steady: private hospitals, government hospitals and export distributors, all of whom consume disposables in proportion to patients treated. Swinging: pharma labs and pathology labs, whose orders follow research budgets, inventory cycles and outbreaks. In between: dentists and households, who follow incomes and online prices.

Now map the tiles onto the doors from card one. Disposables makers sell to the steady tiles, which is why the clock calls hospital disposables barely cyclical. Lab tool makers sell to the swinging tiles, which is why they halved after Covid. Traders sell to households, the tile most exposed to cheap imports.

When you read a device company's results, ask what share of sales comes from each tile, and whether growth is coming from the steady tiles or from a one-off. The so-what line under the grid gives the rule: hospital volumes are the base; lab destocking and outbreaks make the swings.

c4.story:
Strip a device company to its essentials and the first number that matters is gross margin, because it sorts makers from traders more cleanly than anything in the annual report.

A true disposables maker buys polymer, needle tubing and packaging, moulds and assembles them in a clean room, sterilises the result and sells it. The raw materials are a meaningful bite but not the whole meal; a good chunk of each rupee is value the company added itself. In return, it spends on people, power, sterilisation, freight to export markets, and a plant that must be kept to regulator standards.

A trader buys a finished device, often from a Chinese factory, and resells it. Most of each rupee of sales goes straight back to the supplier. What remains is a thin shelf margin, out of which it pays for selling and warehousing. There is very little plant to depreciate, but also very little to protect the margin.

A maker earns a high gross margin and spends it on plants. A trader earns a thin one and spends it on inventory.

The other lines tell you about the cycle. A new plant is a modest build compared with a steel mill or a hospital, but it sits idle for a year or two while customer and regulatory approvals arrive, and depreciation starts the day it opens. Working capital is the quiet danger: distributors hold stock and government buyers pay slowly. After Covid, inventories across the chain ballooned and took about two years to clear, crushing cash flow even where profit looked fine.

Export share brings freight and currency into the picture. When Houthi attacks pushed ships away from the Red Sea route in 2024, freight to Europe became a margin line. And interest matters mostly for small traders funding inventory with working-capital loans; the leaders mostly run net cash.

Finally the line marked no: research spending. It is tiny for Indian listed names, and the explainer is blunt that this is the sector's core weakness.
c4.read:
The two bar charts walk one hundred rupees of sales down to what is left, for a disposables maker and a trader. Start at the left of each and move right.

  • The first bar is the full hundred rupees.
  • The input bar is the clearest difference on the whole page. For the disposables maker, raw materials and components take roughly two-fifths of sales. For the trader, they take about two-thirds, because the trader buys the finished product.
  • The opex bar is people, power, sterilisation, freight and selling: under a third for the maker, about a fifth for the trader, who has no plant to run.
  • The depreciation and interest bar is visible for the maker and a sliver for the trader, the price of owning sterile plants.
  • The last bar is what is left: about a fifth of sales for the maker, under a tenth for the trader. Twice the profit per rupee, earned by doing the manufacturing.

These are illustrative mid-cycle shapes, not any company's accounts; hover a bar for the amounts.

Below, the list marks which lines matter. Gross margin, capex and asset turn, and working capital get a clear yes. Depreciation, export share and freight, and interest get a sometimes. Research spending gets a no, and the reason column explains why that no is a warning rather than a comfort: without research, few Indian device makers own a technology moat.

Use the so-what as a sorting tool: put any device stock's gross margin next to these two shapes and you will know which door it really sits behind.

c5.story:
Hospital disposables barely cycle; people need cannulas in good years and bad. But the rest of the industry rode one of the sharpest boom-busts in recent memory, and the scars still shape how investors value these stocks.

Go back to 2019. Devices were lightly regulated and largely imported, and the government announced it would regulate every device as a drug. Then came Covid. Demand for test kits, pulse oximeters, ventilators, masks, lab plastics and cannulas exploded. Tiny companies with a product anyone needed listed at rich valuations, and the government announced a device incentive scheme and dedicated device parks. In 2021 the pricing authority capped trade margins on oximeters, BP monitors, nebulisers and glucometers, a sign of how hot that market had become. Distributors and labs, terrified of shortages, ordered far more than they needed.

The hangover arrived in 2022. Covid demand vanished, labs sat on mountains of plasticware and kits, and Chinese prices fell. Lab-tool stocks halved. At the same time, licensing became mandatory for every class of device, in phases through 2022 and 2023, which squeezed out small unlicensed importers. The National Medical Devices Policy of 2023 set out a roadmap for local manufacturing.

By 2024 the bottom had passed. Lab destocking ended, hospital volumes stayed strong, and Indian disposables makers started winning export share from China. In 2025 US tariffs on China helped further, while new rules on refurbished machine imports and a component scheme tried to deepen local manufacturing.

Now, in 2026, the industry sits early in a new up-cycle. Hospital bed additions keep disposables demand firm and export capacity is expanding. But price caps on some devices and the pressure of lowest-bid tenders keep margins honest. This is a recovery built on steady consumption rather than another frenzy, which is exactly the kind investors who were burned in 2022 should prefer.
c5.read:
Three pieces work together: the clock, the timeline and the four hands. One caveat from the bold line above the story: hospital disposables barely cycle. The clock mainly describes lab tools, test kits and home devices, riding on a slow structural tailwind of import substitution.

The clock has four arcs: boom at the top right, then peak, bust and bottom going clockwise. The years under each arc mark the Covid loop: boom from 2020 to 2021, peak in 2021, bust from 2022 to 2023, bottom in 2024. The arrow points just before twelve o'clock, at the very end of the bottom arc, about to cross into boom. The label reads early up-cycle. Hover an arc for what defined each phase.

The timeline tells it year by year: neutral for 2019, boom for 2020 to 2021, bust for 2022 to 2023, neutral for 2024 and 2025 as the recovery found its feet, and 2026 marked now.

The four hands let you move the arrow yourself.

  • Hospital surgical volumes: growing steadily, up arrow. The base of demand; a slowdown here is the real warning.
  • Lab inventory at distributors: normalised, up arrow. Rising again would signal another destocking round.
  • Export orders and China pricing: share gains, up arrow.
  • Price caps and tender pricing: a diamond, pressure persists. New caps can compress margins overnight.

Three green hands and one diamond: that is what an early up-cycle looks like, with regulation as the cloud.

c6.story:
For a small device maker in Faridabad or Ahmedabad, the most important decisions are made far away: by a currency market in Mumbai, a factory owner in Zhejiang, a hospital chain's board in Delhi and a trade official in Washington.

Three dials carry the most weight. The first is the rupee, and it cuts both ways. An exporter selling cannulas in dollars and euros earns more rupees when the rupee weakens. But the same company buys polymer and components abroad, and a trader buys finished devices abroad, so a weaker rupee raises their costs. Which effect wins depends on the company's export share and import content.

The second is Chinese device and component prices. China is both the input supplier and the main competitor. When Chinese prices rise, Indian makers become more competitive at home and abroad. When China cuts prices, as it did after Covid, Indian makers lose orders and pricing power at the same time.

The third is hospital bed additions and surgical volumes, the direct driver of disposables demand. With the hospital industry in the middle of its largest bed build in a decade, this dial is a strong and steady tailwind.

Then the two-dot dials. US tariffs on Chinese devices send American orders toward India, a decision that plays out over several quarters as distributors requalify suppliers. Crude oil feeds through to medical-grade polymer prices with a lag. And price caps on devices squeeze margins on whatever gets capped; the stent and knee implant caps of 2017 remain the industry's founding trauma.

The one-dot dials round it out: government health spending lifts tender volumes, at thin margins; pharma research and quality spending drives lab plasticware; and health inflation gives hospitals room to raise prices, a little of which reaches their suppliers.
c6.read:
Each row is one dial. Read across in four steps.

  • Dial: the outside force.
  • Channel: the route by which it reaches profits. Use it to frame questions for the next results call.
  • A rise does: a green up arrow means a rise helps, a red down arrow means it hurts, a diamond means it depends on the company.
  • Weight: one to three dots for how much it matters.

Scan the three-dot rows first. There are three: the dollar against the rupee, marked with a diamond because it helps exporters and hurts importers; Chinese device and component prices, green; and hospital bed additions and surgeries, green. Two of the three heaviest dials are tailwinds right now, which fits the early up-cycle on the clock.

The two-dot rows hold one more tailwind, US tariffs on Chinese devices, and two threats with red arrows: crude oil through polymer costs, and price caps.

The last column shows today's reading where a dial maps to a series we track: the rupee, Brent crude, health inflation, and the pharma index as a rough proxy for pharma research and quality spending. Chinese prices, hospital beds, US tariffs, government spending and price caps show a dash; for those, read hospital chains' bed announcements, trade news and pricing authority notifications.

The so-what line below names the two dials to watch if you watch nothing else: the rupee and Chinese device prices. Between them they set both the cost and the competition. For any company, first work out whether a rupee move helps or hurts it, using its export share and import content.

c7.story:
India makes some of the world's cheapest drugs, so why does it import most of its medical devices? The bottlenecks answer that question.

The first is structural: import dependence. The high-value end, imaging machines, implants, advanced monitors, needs deep engineering, years of clinical data and global service networks. Multinationals dominate it and India imports it. Local makers compete in the low-value end, and even there they often pay import duty on their inputs.

The second is a policy own-goal: the inverted duty structure. Some components attract a higher import duty than the finished device made from them. So it can be cheaper to import a finished product than to import parts and assemble it in India, which punishes exactly the local manufacturing the government wants to encourage.

The third is slow but fundamental: tiny research budgets and small scale. Most listed Indian device makers are small companies that spend little on research, so they rarely own a technology that others cannot copy.

The fourth cuts both ways: regulatory approvals abroad. Clearance from the US FDA, or certification under Europe's stricter Medical Device Regulation, in force since 2021, takes years and serious money. Without it, export growth stalls. With it, a company holds a passport its smaller rivals lack.

Then the recurring irritants. Price caps and lowest-price tenders: when stents were capped in 2017, some multinationals tried to withdraw premium stents from the Indian market and the government moved to stop them. Refurbished imports: cheap used scanners undercut new local equipment, and policy keeps flipping between allowing and restricting them.

And finally the cyclical trap: outbreak-driven swings. Kit and lab demand balloons in an outbreak and collapses afterwards, which misleads anyone who extrapolates a boom year.
c7.read:
Each row is one bottleneck with a reason and a severity label. The label tells you where each risk belongs in your thinking.

  • Structural: import dependence and the inverted duty structure. Permanent, or at least policy-slow, features that keep most listed names at the low-value end. They belong in your valuation.
  • Slow: tiny research spending and scale. A weakness that changes over years, if at all. Watch for the rare company that steps up research spending sustainably.
  • Two-sided: regulatory approvals abroad. A barrier for everyone, and a moat for the few who already hold US and European clearances. When comparing two disposables makers, this row is often the decisive difference.
  • Recurring: price caps and lowest-price tenders, and refurbished imports. The headlines that knock a stock for a week; occasionally a cap reshapes a category.
  • Cyclical: outbreak-driven swings. The reason lab-tool and kit makers halved after Covid, and the reason never to value a company on its outbreak-year earnings.

Read the table as the so-what suggests: the first two rows set a low ceiling on margins for most listed names, and the companies that break through it are the ones with export approvals and real plants, which is the two-sided row turned to advantage.

A practical habit: for each device name you own, note which export approvals it holds. That single fact explains much of the gap in margins and valuations between otherwise similar companies.

c8.story:
For decades, most medical devices in India were barely regulated at all. You could import and sell many of them with little more than a trading licence. That has changed fast, and the changes have shaped who wins.

The Medical Device Rules of 2017 set up a licensing system by risk class, from A for the lowest-risk items to D for the highest-risk ones like heart valves. In 2020 the government brought every device under regulation, and licensing became mandatory for all classes in phases through 2022 and 2023. The effect was a quiet clean-out: small unlicensed importers dropped away, and organised makers with proper plants and paperwork gained share.

Then the pricing authority. Its 2017 caps on coronary stents and knee implants remain the most famous intervention in Indian medtech. In 2021 it capped trade margins on several home devices, oximeters and glucometers among them. Every new cap or trade-margin rule cuts realisations overnight, so this regulator is the one investors watch nervously.

On the encouraging side, the Department of Pharmaceuticals runs the device incentive scheme, the device parks and a newer component scheme, paying makers to build capacity in India. Public procurement rules prefer devices with Indian content, giving local makers an edge in government hospitals. BIS standards and quality control orders put a floor under imports, and environment ministry rules on refurbished equipment, when tight, protect new local machines.

The National Medical Devices Policy of 2023 points further: a roadmap for local manufacturing, research and, eventually, a separate device regulator under its own law, instead of treating devices as a branch of drugs.

And abroad, the US FDA and the European device regulation are the passports to the most profitable markets. A company holding them can sell where margins are highest; one without them is confined to India and smaller export markets.
c8.read:
Each row is a regulator or a rule. Read across: who it is, what it does, why you care, and its status.

The status column is how to prioritise.

  • Always: CDSCO with the Medical Device Rules, and the US FDA with European device regulation. These are the licences to operate at home and to export abroad. They rarely make headlines, but they define who can play.
  • Live: the pricing authority, the Department of Pharmaceuticals, public procurement preference, BIS standards, and the rules on refurbished imports. Five live rows: this is an industry where policy is actively being written. Most of the live rows help local makers; the pricing authority is the exception, and the one to read twice.
  • Coming: the National Medical Devices Policy and its promise of a dedicated device law and regulator. It could change the rules of the game, but on no fixed timeline.

Notice the balance. Almost every row either protects or subsidises the organised Indian maker: licensing removes informal rivals, procurement rules prefer local content, incentive schemes pay for capacity. Against that sits one row, price caps, that can take margin away overnight.

Link this to the call box on card eleven: its first would-change item is a broad price or trade-margin cap on disposables. That is the pricing authority row turning against the core business.

Dated regulatory news, filtered for this industry from our feed, sits on the Picks and signals tab.

c9.story:
Porter's five forces asks one question: once money comes in, who gets to keep it? For medical devices, the honest answer is that the buyer keeps a lot, and the trader keeps very little.

Start with buyers, because they squeeze both doors equally. Hospital chains have procurement teams that bargain hard on every rupee. Government tenders award the contract to the lowest bid. Foreign distributors compare Indian quotes with Chinese ones. A syringe is a syringe, and the buyer knows it.

Where the two doors diverge is in how easy they are to copy. A disposables maker needs a sterile plant, a quality system, an Indian licence and, for the best export markets, US and European approvals. Building that takes years. A trader needs an import licence, a website and a relationship with a Chinese factory, which takes months. So the entrants spoke is where the disposables maker is best protected and the trader most exposed.

Rivalry follows the same logic. The maker competes with China and a handful of Indian peers on cost and reliability. The trader competes with every other importer and every online seller of the same gadget, sometimes sourced from the same factory.

Suppliers squeeze both. Polymer and component makers abroad set input prices for makers. Traders, who often depend on one or two Chinese factories, are more exposed still; if the factory raises prices or sells directly, the trader has nowhere to go.

Substitutes barely trouble the cannula; there is no alternative to putting a tube in a vein. But a branded home device competes with countless cheaper lookalikes online.

Anyone can import the same box. Not everyone can run a sterile plant with a US approval on the wall.
c9.read:
The radar has five spokes, one per force. The further a shape reaches along a spoke, the more pressure that force exerts. So a smaller shape is the better business.

Two shapes are drawn: disposables makers and traders and contract makers. Look at the overall size first. The trader shape is larger on four spokes and level on the fifth. It never comes inside the maker's shape.

  • Entrants: the biggest gap on the chart, one and a half for the maker against three, the maximum, for the trader. Years to build a sterile, approved plant against months to get a trading licence.
  • Rivalry: two against three.
  • Substitutes: one against two. Little replaces a cannula; plenty replaces a branded gadget.
  • Supplier: two against two and a half.
  • Buyer: two and a half for both, the shapes touching. Price-focused hospital buyers and tenders press makers and traders equally hard, and it is the maker's worst spoke.

So the maker's shape is compact except for a bulge toward buyers, while the trader's shape is large and round, exposed everywhere.

The table beside the chart gives each score from zero to three and a reason. The so-what line sums it up: makers with sterile plants and export approvals keep a fair share; traders keep little. If a company you own straddles doors, mentally blend the two shapes by its revenue split, and give extra credit for every export approval it holds.

c10.story:
A small-cap device company's results can be thin on disclosure and heavy on adjectives. Eight numbers cut through it.

Gross margin comes first, because it answers the most important question: is this a maker or a trader? A maker with sterile plants earns a high gross margin; a trader, a thin one. A falling gross margin at a maker means input costs or Chinese competition are biting.

EBITDA margin tells you whether the plants are full and costs under control. Disposables leaders should earn a good margin once outbreak noise is gone; lab tool makers, a bit less.

Export share tells you how exposed the company is to global hospital demand and to the rupee. A healthy share, spread across regions, means the company has the approvals to sell abroad and is not dependent on one market. It is also where the US tariff tailwind shows up.

Sales growth, once Covid distortions are stripped out, is the real test of demand. Disposables leaders should grow steadily as hospital beds and exports expand; a company still below its outbreak-year peak is a lab or kit maker whose demand has not come back.

Then the working-capital pair. Inventory days tell you about destocking risk at distributors and at the company itself; after Covid, this number ballooned across the industry. Receivable days tell you whether tender buyers and distributors are paying on time.

Capex to depreciation tells you whether capacity is being built, and whether it is being built ahead of demand. Pair it with asset turn: building is healthy if each rupee of new plant still generates good sales.

Finally, return on capital: whether the plants earn their cost through a full cycle, outbreak years and hangover years included.
c10.read:
The table has one row per number. Read across: the number, what it tells you, what good looks like, and today's industry median.

  • What it tells you is the question to ask of each company.
  • What good looks like is the benchmark, and the only place on the page with figures. The gross margin and EBITDA rows give separate marks for makers and traders, or for disposables leaders and lab tools. Compare a company with the mark for its own door.
  • Today's industry median comes from the latest annual filings of this industry's listed companies in our database. Seven of the eight rows are mapped to one: everything except export share, which companies disclose in presentations and annual report notes rather than in the standard statements we parse.

A caution on the median: this industry's listed universe is small and skewed toward small companies and traders, so the median sits closer to a typical small company than to the leaders. A leader well above the median on gross margin and return on capital is behaving like a real manufacturer.

The trick is to read three things together for any company: its own number, its door's good mark and the median. Then look at the pairs. Gross margin and inventory days together separate a maker clearing post-Covid stock from a trader stuck with it. Capex to depreciation and return on capital together tell you whether new plants are earning or merely depreciating.

Because most of these companies are small and thinly traded, as the call notes, this table is often the most reliable anchor you have.

c11.story:
For a device maker, the most useful early warnings come from its customers and its competitors' governments, not from its own press releases.

Start with the hospital chains. When Apollo, Max or Medanta announce bed openings and report surgical growth, that is disposables demand a quarter later, because a new bed consumes cannulas, catheters and syringes from the day it opens. Pharma companies' commentary on research and quality spending leads lab plasticware orders by about a quarter. Distributor inventory commentary is the destocking alarm: full channels mean weak orders next quarter, a lesson the lab-tool makers learned the hard way after Covid. And polymer prices reach margins within a quarter.

Some signals act immediately. A pricing authority notification on devices changes realisations from the day it appears. The rupee translates exports and imported inputs at once.

And the signal that speaks furthest ahead comes from Washington. US tariff announcements on Chinese medical goods, like the sharp hike on syringes and needles in 2024, move orders to India only gradually, as distributors qualify new suppliers and run down existing contracts. The effect shows up two quarters or more later.

Put the signals together and you get the rule. The sector is in an up-cycle when hospital volumes are growing, export orders are moving from China to India, and distributor inventories are normal. Two of three means steady growth; one means a pause.

Score it today and all three are on: bed additions continue, tariffs are helping Indian makers, and post-Covid destocking is over. That is why the call is constructive on real manufacturers with export approvals. But it is cautious on traders and on outbreak-era kit makers whose demand never came back, and it reminds you that small, illiquid stocks can run far ahead of earnings in either direction.
c11.read:
The chart places each outside signal by how far ahead it speaks. The further right a dot sits, the earlier the warning. Hover a dot for its channel.

  • Same quarter, far left: pricing authority notifications on devices, and the dollar-rupee rate. These tell you what is already landing.
  • One quarter ahead: hospital chains' bed openings and surgery growth, pharma companies' research and quality commentary, distributor inventory commentary, and polymer prices. The busiest column; read it every quarter in the hospital and pharma results seasons.

Use the chart as a reading order: start on the right, confirm in the middle, treat the left as the scoreboard.

Below sits the three-sign rule. A tick means the sign is on, a cross means it is not, and the note gives today's state. Today all three are ticked: hospital volumes growing with bed additions continuing; exports shifting from China with tariffs helping; distributor inventories normal with destocking over. Three of three is the strongest reading the rule allows, which is why the clock shows an up-cycle rather than a pause.

Finally, the call box gives the headline, three points, and what would change it. Treat the would-change items as alerts: a broad price or trade-margin cap on disposables, a US-China tariff deal that removes India's cost advantage, or a sharp rupee rally that squeezes export margins.
